quotes.text: Whether you think AI will be a fountain of youth or a doomsday technology or something in between, its power — both present and potential — is indisputable. Its capacity to cure diseases or produce bioweapons, to protect against the most advanced cyberattacks or hack the most robust technological fortresses, to foster shared prosperity for the many or to amass unimaginable wealth for the few, are each different sides of the same coin: significant capacity that can lead to superhuman power.
No concentration of such power — whether it be in an individual, a company, a nation, or a technology — can be allowed to go unchecked or unrestrained. And it certainly cannot go unregulated.

Since I entered Congress, I’ve been calling on my colleagues to meet this moment and to marshal our collective power to regulate AI. It’s why, as a member of the Science, Space, and Technology Committee, I’m pushing for regulations domestically and, as a member of the Foreign Affairs Committee, I’ve argued for an “arms control” approach to AI globally. We need human-centric laws that protect our economy, our finances, our privacy, our health, our democracy, and, yes, our existence.

The government absolutely has to regulate artificial intelligence so that we’re maximizing the potential that it has to expand access to health care and improve health outcomes while also mitigating the risk. [...] We can’t stick our heads in the sand and pretend like this innovation is not without any risk.

It was wonderful to further get to know new colleagues on both sides of the aisle while hearing from brilliant minds studying some of the biggest issues of the day.

“Artificial intelligence is shaping everything from how hospitals manage data to how small businesses streamline tasks,” said Rep. McBride. “But right now, only big tech companies have the manpower and capacity to steadily compile and release information about the AI models they build and deploy. Smaller teams — including government agencies, schools, and nonprofits — are left guessing and may lack the resources to accomplish the same.

The READ AI Models Act brings transparency to AI in a way that’s simple, consistent and accessible. Think of it as a clear, easy-to-read snapshot — a ‘nutrition label’ for an AI model. It levels the playing field and helps people make informed decisions.

Just a warning: there's been a spike in AI slop about me online lately, including fake images and completely fabricated quotes, often about gender. They pop up on your feed from these "content farms" and can even seem innocuous, but they're meant to foster division and spread false information and inaccurate perceptions.

AI can look incredibly real, but don’t believe everything at first glance. If it's from a page or source that you don't recognize, take a moment to double-check what you’re seeing or sharing.

AI is certainly the biggest change in society since the Industrial Revolution. And I would argue, potentially, is the biggest change in society since humans went from a nomadic species to an agriculturally based, stationary species. I mean, it's that significant in not just how our economy works, but how we relate to one another.

I am someone who believes in what we call sectoral regulation. I think regulation for AI looks different in agriculture than it does in transportation, than it does in education, than it does in healthcare.

A new quarter, a new wave of AI bot farmed spread disinformation about me. Nearly 9k retweets on a quote I never said.

This will slowly transfer over to other platforms. And circulate there for a few weeks on different content farms. Rinse, repeat. 

A lot of this is bots talking to bots, but it’s pervasive.

I am not ignorant to the competition with China on AI, but there is simply no realistic risk that we do too much when it comes to regulating AI. I mean, have you seen Congress? 

The risk is clearly that we do too little -- and that risk is too great to bear.

You have whistleblowers warning us and AI CEOs admitting the risk, endorsing a slow down, and calling for meaningful oversight. Truly what excuse would Republican politicians have to resist what is obviously and existentially urgent? https://t.co/0LelUGWgxq
